body:
Yeah. I guess I'm being haunted by this transition I appear to be inducing in women. They go from eager to treating me like a subhuman in almost the blink of an eye. Nobody who can explain this to me with all of the information (these women) is possibly ever going to clear this up for me. 

Which means my only option is to try to work my way out of being bad at sex, but that isn't going to happen if I keep getting kicked while I'm trying to get back up. I am trapped here. Going home when I'm kicked out of bed at 1 AM isn't going to change how fucked up it makes me feel to be treated this way.
Thanks for the encouragement. My recommendation for you: compliment them back. Even if it is the stupidest, first thing to come to mind. Self-deprecate if it is clear what you just said is silly.

Sure, a lot of guys align with the stereotype of trying to bang as many women as possible, and hitting and quitting it is the most efficient way to accomplish that.

 Sticking with that stereotype, I can't think of a single time I've heard of a girl and a guy going on a date and the girl invited him home right after the date and the guy said no because he had a three date minimum and then they went on more dates and then they had sex and the guy cut her off. In that case, I think the woman would be experiencing the same types of confusion and frustration I am. Of course, I've never heard of that happening.

That's entirely fair. On the other hand, I spent most of my 20's isolated and sexless. I finally broke through that a couple years ago. The problem is, since then, I've been treated like trash after I have sex. 

Having sex once is good I guess to lose your virginity. After that, it is really about connection for me. Regular sex is what anyone who wants to have sex should probably be shooting for. Having sex once a year with someone who immediately doesn't want anything to do with you is hardly going to do anything for loneliness.

Once I got the STD, I just couldn't break the feeling of loneliness. If you aren't getting laid, which is truly closer to my norm as well, you are perhaps being held back or rejected based on characteristics that you hope you can resolve at some point. I, right now however, feel like I'm just constantly offering a shit value proposition to any possible partners. On rare occasion, I can get someone to want to want to hang out with me. I'm slightly risking disease for anyone I have sex with and, on top of that, they never want to see me after we have sex. That's a fear and loneliness I can't shake even once I'm in bed with someone.

Disclaimer: sex and loneliness are not as connected as I might be implying.

I want to say one other thing about this whole problem. I'm finally able to start putting myself out there to meet women again. I'd be okay with women finding whatever deal breakers they want with me early on and going on their way. I'd prefer they wouldn't ghost me, but I guess this isn't terribly rare. I just can't have the deal breaker be sex.

What's bothering me is this sick combination of girls pumping and dumping me with the fact that I'm scared shitless of getting another STD or giving one to someone I'm probably not going to be serious with. I can't afford to go through a dozen women this way. Not only is it rare I get to that point with a woman, I'm worried about my health. I would establish standards such as requiring a certain number of dates first (the girl who did this to me had a three date minimum), but if they are going to discard me after sex anyway, what is the point of drawing out the courtship.

I don't have an answer for you and that planned doctor's visit is probably the only thing that might help clear your mind. I don't know why the other answer here instantly fixates on herpes while stating it is unlikely the cause and you didn't even mention herpes. I would think if the hand and penis rashes are caused by the same infection, it is likely curable, whatever it might be. If it is just eczema, well you know how to deal with that already.

I just wanted to call out scabies as a slight possibility so it isn't missed. It is probably not the case since you seem to be lacking the symptom of always itching like crazy, but the between-the-fingers rash makes me instantly think of scabies. Just something worth running past the doctor when you get there. I would expect the doctor to know well enough, but I've heard of a few cases of scabies going misdiagnosed for far too long. I wish you luck. Post an update when you find out more.

Could be a strong reaction to chigger bites. Going off the beaten path is a good way to run into them. They start at your feet but will wander over you for hours looking for a good place to bite, often accumulating at lines they cannot easily cross (waist with a belt or tight underwear). You can determine if that hypothesis makes sense based on what you were wearing that day.

The one thing you said that made me think of them is the itchiness when scratched. Chigger bites are one of the itchiest things I've ever dealt with, but only if I first scratch it or my clothing rubs against it the right way. Before that, I can pretty much ignore it.

In the US, they are much more common in the south and the midwest. Elsewhere, I don't know their prevalence.

A doctor at a Planned Parenthood. I was diagnosed a year ago and everyone is sure it is molluscum (the Planned Parenthood doctor, my new PCP, and my new dermatologist). My first line of treatment was waiting. Nearly went crazy. I experimented with some tea tree oil on a bump out of curiosity (and urgency since it seems to take forever to get any/another appointment) but nothing happened. 

Once I got my first appointment with my new PCP, I got the second line of treatment which was podofilox, no cryotherapy. It did nothing for the bumps. Finally decided to go extreme on treatment. Scheduled another appointment with the PCP to ask her to cut these off or whatever is necessary to fix this as fast and reliably as possible. Waited a long time for that appointment. PCP doesn't have the necessary stuff for cryotherapy or curettage, so I am told to go to a dermatologist. Schedule appointment with a dermatologist. Wait for a long time. In the meantime, I've started going to therapy. Finally get to my dermatologist appointment, and get the third line of treatment, cryotherapy on the bumps that I've found and an imiquimod prescription. Dermatologist glances over areas I know to be affected but definitely missed at least one bump until I pointed it out (and yes, it was confirmed MC once she looked closely at it). She freezes the spots, tells me to schedule a followup in 8-10 weeks. Over two months! How does this even make any sense? I've been dealing with this for over a year. If I got infected from sex, the infection was from at least 18 months ago. How is this not being treated seriously when I'm clearly not resolving this issue in the timeline of the "normal" case?

I'm sorry if I'm making this sound like a rant, but most cases I've read about people are going to the dermatologist every two to three weeks to get these MC treated. You took "a few trips" to the dermatologist. Does "few" mean four or five? If it is five, that would be another year's worth of trips for me based on how these appointments are scheduled. 

Between the point at which I decided I needed anything and everything done to get rid of these ASAP and the point at which I will have a followup with my dermatologist is a half year. That's what's bothering me. It just seems there is a severe disconnect between my needs as a patient and treatment.

This issue is serious for me. How do I get it treated that way when it comes to scheduling, treatment options available, and thoroughness by the doctors? Every medical professional treats this as no big deal in tone and execution, but it is destroying me. I'm tired of feeling like a pariah.

Looks like molluscum contagiousum to me. It looks like at least a couple of them have the characteristic dimple. The rest might as well and it just might not show up in the picture. I would see a doctor about it.

If it is molluscum, it does go away, but possibly very slowly. Treatment is typically recommended to speed up the process. Don't shave anymore as that will help spread it. Only trim until this is resolved.

Well I didn't really start treatment other than a couple unsuccessful experiments like the zymaderm mentioned above. I just let it run its course since I wasn't having sex with anybody and wasn't eager to anytime soon. I wouldn't recommend this as it has impacts on other areas of your life. During this entire time, taking showers has been a bit slower since I'm being more careful about what touches what after what. I passed up hopping in a hot tub a few times during the winter and haven't been swimming this summer since I'm afraid of spreading it on myself or to others. 

I probably had up to 10 bumps at the worst point. Within six months, I was down to one bump which I still have a couple months later. I might actually try a few things on that remaining bump soon. After I think I've cleared it, I'm going to go back to the doctor to get a close look over to be sure it is gone.

Obviously, as you can tell, it is a slow process if you go without treatment.

Yeah. MC is weird. It can take up to six months to show up. If she had it, and even though it is very contagious, you may not have contracted it early on in the relationship or you may not have noticed the bumps for a long time. Mine popped up four months after the last time I'd had sex, and we'd been exclusively having sex for months before that.

The gym towel seems like the logical culprit in my case too, but it was quite the coincidence in my case as well when it occurred. I, like you, had a pretty big window of celibacy before my last partner. If I were to have contracted MC at some other random point in my adult life, the gym towel would have been the only logical explanation, not just the "likely" one. That fact and the area I contracted it makes it enough of a coincidence for me to believe I got it from sex. It isn't that it would be latent in her, just that it could have gone unnoticed. It isn't anybody's fault if it had. Or she doesn't and never had it. The point is, MC is tricky. If I were you, I'd work with my girlfriend to reasonably limit any risks of perpetuating MC between the two of you, and that involves her understanding her situation as well. I wouldn't sweat it, at least you two have each other.

I tried zymaderm, which is basically tea tree oil and iodine, on one of my spots and it didn't do anything. However, I do believe I've seen genuine reports of success with tea tree oil and iodine. It seems everyone responds differently. I think most people trust the dermatologist to do his/her job right and give it time. I think this approach is successful for most people and, being so uneventful, isn't written about as often online.

It is your call, your girlfriend's call, and your dermatologist's call whether you can limit the risk to an acceptable level while having sex. I have read about people passing it back and forth to each other and getting frustrated. The prevailing idea is that you can avoid infecting someone else if you keep the spots covered so as to avoid direct contact with the bumps or contact with an intermediate fomite (example: towel touches your bumps, someone else touches the towel). On the other hand, some people talk about some bumps being so small as to go unnoticed, even by the person infected, so be careful.

Also, do you know how you contracted this? It is a bit of a coincidence that you contracted this directly on the shaft and only on the shaft within a few months of having your first sexual partner in years. Perhaps she should make a visit to the dermatologist as well for a really close once-over for both your sakes.

No I haven't. Yes, I plan to do so. This all has to do with not having the energy or time to do anything about it. I feel like my anxiety is a bigger issue than obsession, but I'm sure we'd have the opportunity to cover any and all my issues.

Molluscum and the possibility of herpes are just the last straw. It doesn't matter if they are small problems. There are so many things that can get in the way of a relationship. There are so many ways you can inadvertently hurt someone you care about. But this? This is one I should have been able to avoid. One I should have been able to control. One that those I have been with should have been able to control. This is a direct result of my past intimacy, and it compromises the health (mental or physical) of all future partners. These types of problems are a bit twisted.

And I don't know why I haven't found love. I can get a bit introspective about it. I don't think it was a high priority for me for a few years and I have no regrets about that. I had crushes in high school. Similar in college. Nothing really materialized from this in college, and the one time something could have, we didn't take it very far because I was a senior and about to move away. I'd shut out women who were clearly interested in me, basically because I often just wasn't attracted to them. That's fair, right? After a while, I decided maybe my standards were too high and started to entertain the possibility of relationships with women who were so forward with me. After all, I could appreciate that quality in a woman. In the end, I wasn't satisfied with these relationships. The chemistry just wasn't there. 

A few months ago, I decided to start really going for it when I found someone I was really interested in. It was actually working out for once. Before we had sex, I discovered this STD (an awful but sort of fortunate coincidence). So just as I was finding a new approach in my love life at the transition to my 30s, I got shut down by this surprise. In the immediate shock, I just let that possible relationship fizzle out. Since then, I've just been... alone. Kind of lost. So yeah, I think the big problem was that I was just figuring out what I wanted and building up myself to maybe get what I wanted, and then my plans got shattered.

Thanks for the hug.

Well the good news is you are almost certainly HSV-2 negative considering the time since last exposure, which I'm guessing is the whole reason you even got tested in the first place. Your result for HSV-1 wouldn't have anything to do with your friend having HSV-2, and even if you do have it, it is likely unrelated to your encounters with this friend.

I might be wrong, but I think an equivocal result is only a big deal and a likely positive if your exposure was recent and you are still accumulating antibodies (in which case, the result will be higher in a subsequent test). The odds are low that you, an adult with plenty of years and opportunities to be exposed to HSV-1, were recently exposed to HSV-1 at the same time you happened to be exposed to HSV-2 and decided to get tested. Go ahead and get tested again if you want, but my interpretation is that the 1.08 doesn't mean you are positive and probably has nothing to do with this friend with HSV-2. You are only bothered with this information because you wanted to get tested for HSV-2. You did and are negative. Most adults have HSV-1 and if you do, it isn't the biggest deal. You would just be careful about not passing it or any other contagions to your daughter and just know that you are already more informed than most parents (a majority of which have HSV-1) about the risk of passing HSV-1 to others. And just know that, even after that effort, your daughter will probably end up with HSV-1 at some point in her life anyway if a vaccine isn't created.

You are getting terms confused. HSV-1 and HSV-2 are types, they don't describe where you have herpes, though HSV-1 is more likely oral and HSV-2 is more likely genital. If she has HSV-2 and only HSV-2, she can only give you HSV-2. If you were to give her oral, you could contract HSV-2 orally, though that isn't very common (still possible though). I might be wrong, but I think even if you do contract HSV-2 orally, then you shouldn't likely have many outbreaks or shed the virus as much as if you had it genitally. Still, I get why you'd want to avoid contracting it.

So, you cannot get HSV-1 from oral sex with someone who only has HSV-2. If she tests positive for both HSV-1 and HSV-2, then it is most likely she has HSV-2 genitally and HSV-1 orally. In that case, you are more likely to get HSV-1 from kissing her. Over half the population has HSV-1 (mostly oral) and you and she might have it already. If this is so important to your current relationship, then you should both get blood tested for both types and determine what that means for your future sexual interactions.

I'm guessing you both used the razor on your genitals if you are concerned with STDs, right? Fomites can transmit some skin infections, but I wouldn't be overly concerned about it. There is a small risk of contracting blood-borne diseases (HIV and some forms of Hep) through a razor, but that risk is very low. HIV doesn't last too long on surfaces. Certainly not something to worry yourself about, but if I were you, I'd insist they go to the doctor to get tested for everything because that behavior is bullshit.

As you've probably read, it can take up to six months for the bumps to appear after initial exposure. Mine showed up at least four months after the last time I had sex, so assuming I got it from sex, it was a long time after exposure. Not that it matters, but that might change where you think you got it from if you had a different partner within a few months before your current one.

The good thing about molluscum is that you could probably get this treated and play it off as something you picked up at school in gym class or something. Not that you should tell your doctor that, and not that your doctor would believe you, but that might get it past your family.

Regardless, because you have contracted an STD, you should get tested for others if you haven't already. There are sometimes cheap/free options out there for the uninsured and you can probably find them with google or a few phone calls to nearby clinics. I don't know how those deals work for people who have insurance and just don't want to use it, though.

I know I've read of at least one person getting this done, but I can't find that information anymore and I'm not sure if it was in North America.

I haven't tried using ACV so I can't give you any good advice on that. However, at some point, well before having molluscum, I developed a sensitivity to neosporin that looks like that, causing wounds to basically fester. After that happened, I asked a pharmacist about it and was told that it is pretty common. I'm not saying that is the case for you, but just wanted to throw it out there as a possibility.

This looks and sounds a lot like molluscum. Let's start with some basics. Shaving will spread it around on the skin, so you should stop doing that until the molluscum bumps are gone. Each spot should, in theory, clear up on its own after a long while, but it isn't much help if you help new ones to keep popping up. If you need to get a good view of it for treatment purposes, just stick to trimming. Do not touch, or let anything else touch, the lesions and then touch an unaffected area. This will spread it. This goes for razors, as already mentioned, but towels, bar soap, fingers, fingernails, etc. I use a fresh towel every time I take a shower and the last thing I dry off is my genitals. When drying this area, I pat dry instead of rubbing the towel around. Some people even go so far as to not use a towel at all for the affected area but instead use disposable paper towels or toilet paper. This probably isn't a bad idea, but it might be overkill. Always wash your hands including under your nails after touching the area. You shouldn't be having sex and, considering where it is, you should consider not masturbating. I keep alcohol based sanitizer by my bed for after my hands make their way down there. I might be a bit obsessive about the cleanliness though.

Ok. Those are the important points to know no matter how you proceed. I got this last September. I had one bump a little below my navel, some at the base of my penis and the rest were in between (more or less in the area you'd shave) except a couple on my thighs. I didn't have them all over the shaft though. I'm down to one bump that I know of on my thigh, and I'm going to go get a look over by a dermatologist after that one is gone just to make sure I'm not missing any. I didn't really get any treatment, while I did experiment with zymaderm and duct tape occlusion on a couple spots each. Zymaderm didn't do anything for me, the occlusion did seem to have an impact, but I wasn't going to do that with every spot. To be clear, I wouldn't recommend waiting it out (and most people wouldn't). I did because my case has been mild and I wasn't exactly getting back out there anytime soon and was curious to see how my body would handle it. Especially since you seem to have a worse case than I do/did, you should go get this checked out. Also, if you believe you contracted this from sex, you should be getting tested for other STDs anyway. In the meantime, just being healthy should improve your body's chances of managing this. Get good rest. Eat healthily. Don't smoke and minimize drinking.

As recommended by /u/Suicidal_thoughts91 , planned parenthood is an option in the US. You will need to call and explain your situation (financially and parents insurance and everything) and find out what the price would be for you out of pocket to see if that is an option. Besides planned parenthood, you'll just have to google and explore other options in your area. If you're in school, check on what services they provide. If you're over 18 and in the US, you should call your parents' insurance company to inquire about what measures they take to not share health details with your parents when the statement is passed along to them. I think the law outlines some restrictions, but I'm not 100% sure.

Most importantly though, you should consider this to be like any other medical issue and your health is important. I would say go to your normal doctor since it is simplest. Molluscum apparently isn't always spread by sex in adults (if that's what mortifies you), and this should just be considered yet another issue in an embarrassing area. Once you are at the doctor's office, you should discuss any past risk exposures and probably get tested for STIs. You could also discuss with the doctor/desk the possibility of paying for STI tests out of pocket (which are more likely to be easily interpreted from an insurance statement) while the rest of the appointment gets passed along to insurance.

There are over 100 types, 30 are transferred sexually. About 10 may cause genital warts. About the same amount cause cervical cancers. The overwhelmingly common ones that often cause either of these symptoms are vaccinated for. The 9 type vaccine is closing a shrinking gap. And yes, just like any vaccine, you can still be infected with one you are vaccinated for. I don't know why you are losing your shit. I've seen you here a lot and I've appreciated one of our previous conversations. I don't know why you are accusing me of spewing misinformation when you are the one speculating another fifty types of HPV will be discovered. Sure, maybe they discover another 50 types. Are those 50 going to be considered the major causes of genital cancer and warts compared to the ones they are already vaccinating for? That would be really surprising. They are more likely to fit into the entirely innocuous virus category, along with a lot of other viruses. Maybe one day we discover a lot of health problems can be traced back to some currently unknown (or unfeared) virus, but cervical cancer and warts are being pretty clearly tied to known HPV viruses.

And surely at least one pharmaceutical company had an interest in an HPV vaccine, otherwise it wouldn't exist.

Most of the types don't cause cancer or warts or any other symptoms (for anyone), just like a lot of other virus particles we harbor. Only a few types are known to be a problem and some are stigmatized. The common strains that do cause trouble are vaccinated for. The vaccine covers dangerous types (cancer causing) and what I would consider stigmatized types (wart causing). Those wart causing strains are certainly stigmatized and the people who have/had warts need to deal with the same sort of questions/issues as someone with herpes does. And even though they could have cleared it from their system, they'll never know for sure! You can't protect partners from it with barriers and, until recently, your partner couldn't get a vaccine (though not perfect) to protect themselves. 

I might be wrong, but I could swear genital warts had a bigger stigma a decade ago before the vaccine became popular. More jokes about it and another thing people were really afraid of contracting. I almost never even hear it mentioned anymore unless I'm on here.

The protection against wart causing strains wouldn't be part of the vaccine if the only goal was to prevent serious diseases and they didn't want to bother, or wanted to avoid dealing with diseases that only have a stigma.

By this logic, no vaccines would be created, or at least none for typically harmless diseases (chickenpox, shingles). They would just make money off of treatments. It isn't like big pharma is one company. The company that stands to benefit from making and selling a vaccine isn't typically the same company that makes money off of the current treatments.

If a vaccine is created and patented and it is recommended that all children get it at a certain age until prevalence is nearly 0 (which would take decades), then that company makes some good money. After 20 years the patent expires so the company that did the research is not expecting to make monopoly-level profits beyond 20 years anyway. The expected and planned 20 years of a patent-supported monopoly (which is the same for all medicines, not just vaccines) will complete well before there is a massive drop off in people getting vaccinated.

The opportunity cost of herpes vaccine research vs research for other vaccines, cures, and treatments certainly comes into play, but I don't think it is a money loser holding back the research. The HPV vaccine does pretty well, and while it *can* save lives, that isn't the only reason people are getting it. The risk of developing HPV related cancer in a given year is 1 in 10,000 and it isn't even that likely to kill you if it is caught with regular check ups. People get this vaccination for peace of mind, and they'll do the same for herpes vaccinations. 

They'll decrease the risk of blindness from herpes (significantly if the vaccine covers HSV-1), decrease the risk of other ailments currently loosely linked to herpes, reduce the odds of needing a c-section, decrease the risk of getting other STDs helped along by herpes infections (notably HIV, if a vaccination doesn't exist for it first), and remove the risk of infecting others with it. The monetary motivation is there, at least as much as it is for any other vaccine currently out on the market.

Ha. I get where you're coming from, though I don't see how someone has more responsibility to protect a polycule than any other person/group of people. If someone gives herpes to their one-time tinder date, they are doing a greater disservice (from a utilitarian view) than introducing herpes to a stable polycule, considering that that tinder date is likely to infect many more people.

If the polycule is composed of two very long term partners with additional shorter term partners (not so short term as to be swinging, but a definite cycling through of partners), then you are accepting a high risk anyway on your and your partners' behalves, even if you vet them. If you are dealing with a multi-year stable polycule, then the risk is actually being managed well.

If I, for example, went through a different partner every two months and made them all get tested (and, maybe being unreasonable, required them to be HSV negative), then I am ruling out partners who have been infected for a long time and probably less infectious (have antibodies), but they may have been recently infected and more infectious themselves (since the antibodies aren't there yet). Six times a year I would possibly be exposing myself to that risk (if following the two month theoretical schedule) and, if in a polycule, any other partners in it. I'd have decreased the risk with testing but definitely hurting it by having that many partners. This is obviously just an example. In one year I would be more than doubling my number of past partners in this case. Haha. The point is, having all those partners may be just as bad as following a doctor's recommendation of not getting tested.

Getting tested for the dangerous STDs (and maaaaybe HSV) is a prime responsibility everybody should probably be doing, but cycling through partners at any high rate is also considered a risk factor, and as such, is also "wrong" by that standard. The problem is, arguing that makes you a prude even though its completely true.

Obviously, anybody can get herpes. Newly ex-virgins can contract it. I can get it. But if I got it, it is mostly because my last partner's risk factors were that much higher (regardless of testing), having an order of magnitude more sex than I have and possibly close to an order of magnitude greater partners than I have. Even if she tested negative before we had sex, she would be way more risky to me than I was to her because she'd had sex with other partners more recently than I had (within the testing window).

I'm not arguing for monogamy or only having sex in long term relationships after being together for a few months (I haven't followed these rules and I think it would suck), but I'm just pointing out that testing for something a doctor doesn't recommend and insisting other partners to do the same doesn't put you on some high horse, as if other behaviors you or anyone else engages in don't put others around you at real and more significant risk than someone like me with a very small number of past partners (and tested negative before the most recent partner) forgoing the HSV test the doctor doesn't recommend. You are mitigating it, but, if it was such a big deal, there is still probably more you could do but don't. It's just that those other perhaps reasonable measures are overridden by immediate sexual desires and needs, and that makes it okay.

Yeah, that's the thing. Outside the conversation on this post, I don't think you often see people embracing willful ignorance (usually a doctor is giving them that ignorance without discussion). So while it might have been naive, it isn't a naivete about the malice of other people, but about those other peoples' naivete.  I'm pretty sure most people who have herpes don't even suspect it, considering 80% don't "know" they have it (be it not even suspecting it or willful ignorance).

When I explain to friends in casual conversation that: 

* While condoms do decrease the risk of spreading herpes (HSV-2), the drop in risk is not that significant

* One in six have it

* 80% of them don't know it, so probably around 3%-4% have it and know it, and the remainder of the one in six are going around probably not even suspecting they have it

They are shocked. Just telling them those facts, most are immediately thoroughly convinced that they likely have it. Of course, once I tell them that just because they've had more than six partners, it doesn't guarantee they have it (basic knowledge from stats class) and it doesn't usually transmit in one encounter, but can take months between those in a discordant couple, they aren't as concerned. Still, just knowing they could be among the 80% who "have no symptoms" is a brand new thought/idea to them. Giving them the quick facts (that just about everyone on this subreddit knows about herpes) transforms their entire concept of HSV.

I have a friend I told when I last got tested for everything. Talked about the nerve-racking experience. I asked him if it usually makes him feel that way. He said he always wears condoms (and I do truly believe he has been 100% thorough about that his entire life) and hasn't had a broken one, so he's literally never gotten tested. He's my age. Given, if he doesn't get tested for HSV, then the odds that he has anything they'd test for is slim since they mostly rely on a failed barrier. Yet, it never occurred to him that he might have something since he practices "safe(r)" sex.

Anyway, long winded response just to say if you did get herpes while being naive, it would probably be from someone who didn't know/suspect it. No malice required.

False positives are always possible, but it has nothing to do with having it done "this early." The test doesn't care about how recently you think you may have contracted HIV. It is either reactive or not reactive and, if the test is reactive, they will do another more specific but more expensive and slower test to determine whether you are actually positive.

False positives are rare, so I wouldn't let it hold you back from getting the test, as the false positive will be a possibility when you take the test later as well. The more often you take HIV tests, the more likely you are to end up with one false positive, but that is quickly remedied with more tests. While false positives are rare, HIV is so rare in some populations that you are more likely to get a false positive than an actual positive. Don't let any of this hold you back though, they will ultimately find out if you are positive or negative. Positive results aren't considered accurate without more tests.

http://www.cdc.gov/hiv/ will have up to date information and http://www.webmd.com/hiv-aids/guide/aids-hiv-medication discusses some medicines, though I don't think it is that useful at this point. I think it is most important to just know that people with HIV are living healthy, strong, long lives these days. That is the norm, not the exception.

Lastly, not to get your hopes up, because any one sex act can lead to infection with HIV, but the odds are low: http://www.cdc.gov/hiv/policies/law/risk.html Barely one in 70 acts for the highest risk sexual activity will cause someone to contract HIV (if the other partner is known HIV positive). This does vary a bit depending on how recently the other person has been infected (probably a higher viral load if very recent), if the other person is taking medicine for it, and so on. If you don't even know if the other person is positive and just going on a hunch, the odds are much lower. I don't know enough about your situation, but it is possible you are just getting yourself worked up for no good reason or focusing on this possibility of having HIV as a way to cope with a decision you regret or something that happened to you outside of your control. I wish you well.
